author: TEDx Talks
description:
Can two people hear the same sound and experience it completely differently? This speaker uses the science of music and sound perception to challenge our assumptions about reality itself. Drawing on the groundbreaking research of psychoacoustics pioneer Diana Deutsch, Emilia reveals how our brains actively interpret sound through the lens of our language, culture and personal experiences. From musical illusions such as the Tritone Paradox to the powerful connection between music, memory and emotion, she explores why the same melody can evoke different feelings in different people. She argues that our unique perspectives shape how we understand conversations, relationships and the world around us. By recognising that others may genuinely experience the same moment differently, we can approach disagreement with greater empathy and understanding. ‘Same Sound, Different Worlds’.
With her passion for intellectual exploration, Emilia particularly enjoys French, history and maths, and is fas
title: Same sound, different worlds | Emilia Rasulova | TEDxSt Swithuns School

author: TEDx Talks
description:
How much do we really know about a person after a single glance? In this powerful and deeply personal talk, the speaker reveals how snap judgements formed in fractions of a second can shape the lives of people with visible differences. Using her own experience of growing up with a cleft lip and palate, alongside examples from popular culture and psychological research, Sophie explores how media representations influence unconscious bias. From film villains with facial scars to real-world discrimination, she examines how stereotypes are carried into everyday interactions and invites us to see the person behind the face. ‘Face Value’.
As STEM Ambassador at St Swithun’s, Sophie enjoys encouraging younger students to engage with science and explore new ideas. She is particularly interested in the relationship between biology and psychology, especially how these disciplines shape perception and behaviour. Outside the classroom, she is competing in the European Space Agency’s CanSat competi
title: Face value | Sophie Casey | TEDxSt Swithuns School

author: TEDx Talks
description:
From Stanley Cups and skincare trends to late-night TikTok purchases, this talk examines how consumer culture is being reshaped by the rise of digital payments and life without cash. Questioning what society stands to lose in a cashless future, the speaker explores the hidden value of cash as a tool for privacy, independence and financial inclusion. Through examples ranging from online algorithms and targeted advertising to data breaches and consumer surveillance, Natalie reveals how digital transactions can influence spending habits and generate vast amounts of personal data. She also highlights the challenges a fully cashless society could create for vulnerable groups including older people, those living in poverty, and individuals seeking financial privacy. The talk invites audiences to look beyond convenience and consider a bigger question: as technology transforms the way we spend, how much privacy, freedom and control are we willing to trade away? ‘Cashless - At What Cost?’.

title: Cashless - At what cost? | Natalie Yiu | TEDxSt Swithuns School

description:
This thought-provoking talk traces the origins of the concept of Orientalism, examining how literature, art, tourism and politics have shaped Western perceptions of the East for centuries. Beginning with the myth of Shangri-La and moving through colonial history, Egyptian tourism and influential works of art, the speaker reveals how entire regions and cultures have been reduced to romanticised fantasies. Anissa draws on the work of scholar Edward Said to explore how these narratives extended beyond storytelling, influencing political attitudes, social stereotypes and global power structures. By questioning whose stories are told, who is telling them, and whose interests they serve, Anissa challenges us seek a deeper, more authentic understanding of the world. ‘The Myth of the Orient’.
Anissa is fascinated by the law and global affairs. With a love of debate, MUN and mooting, she particularly enjoys exploring questions on public law, such as constitutional rights, regulation and the li
title: The Myth of the Orient | Anissa Sim | TEDxSt Swithuns School

description:
Shakespeare’s words remain instantly recognisable more than four centuries after his death so why do many young people struggle to connect with his plays? This young speaker argues that Shakespeare’s works have lost none of their relevance but that the way we present them must evolve. Drawing on personal experience, modern theatre productions, and examples from contemporary society, Eliza-Grace shows how reimagining Shakespeare’s plays in familiar settings can help new audiences engage with his timeless themes of love, conflict, leadership and unity. She makes the case for greater access to live theatre and more opportunities for young people to experience Shakespeare as it was intended: performed, not simply read.  ‘Much Ado About Relevance’.

title: Much ado about relevance | Eliza-Grace Suswain | TEDxSt Swithuns School

author: TEDx Talks
description:
In life, what is your North? Is it a place on any map? Or is it the quiet pull you feel towards a happy and good life, lived your own way? Most of us sense it long before we can name it.
The harder part is finding the roads that lead there, when life gives us no guide and no perfect plan.
Most of us are handed a map for our lives by others. Many of its routes are useful because they have worked for the people who travelled those roads before us. But what do you do when something inside you says, “I don’t want to go this way”?
Navigating life’s unwritten map is about discovering your own direction. It is about creating your own compass, learning to trust it, and moving towards your purpose even when the road ahead is unclear.
In this talk, Priyadarshi Siddharth shares how he learned to listen to his inner compass and what to do when the map and the compass disagree.
The road can change. Your North does not have to.
 Co-founder at DreamVid Creatives and Ex-VP at BYJU'S. A pioneer of vis
title: When your map and compass disagree | Priyadarshi Siddharth | TEDxGWH School Bannerghatta

author: TEDx Talks
description: The education system is a mill, and its product has just been made worthless. Generative AI now does — faster and better — nearly everything schools spend fifteen years drilling into children: the recall, the formulas, the essays, the credentials. We are still marching students through an assembly line built for a world that no longer exists. So a brutal question remains: when the machine can do it all, what is actually left worth learning? This talk argues we must tear up the blueprint. Start with the child and expand outward — through the neighborhood, the region, the planet, and back and forth in time — so that learning is anchored in the real, messy world the child lives in, not a syllabus written in some distant center. The skill that survives is the human one: navigating complexity that no model can hand you. And AI, far from the threat we're scrambling to control, becomes the most powerful companion for the adventure at hand. Stop preparing children for life. Let school be life
title: Last Things Worth Learning | Manohar Swaminathan | TEDxGWH School Bannerghatta

description: In this eye-opening talk, Dr. Kaitlin Devaney challenges our conventional understanding of violence by asking a crucial question: what if the most consequential forms of harm are the ones we cannot easily see? Drawing on research and community-based work in Chicago, Devaney examines how structural conditions—such as systemic disinvestment, segregation, and institutional neglect—quietly perpetuate violence long before a crisis appears. By shifting the focus away from individual blame and toward the power structures that dictate policy and opportunity, this talk opens vital new pathways for social change, policy reform, and collective responsibility. Kaitlin Devaney is a Research Specialist at UIC’s Institute for Research on Race and Public Policy. Her work examines community violence, structural inequities, and systems of accountability. In this inspiring talk, Neel Patel invites audiences to rethink how they approach major, life-defining decisions by shifting focus from what choice to make to who they want to become. Drawing from personal turning points—from selecting a college major on a whim to navigating an unexpected corporate layoff—Patel challenges the paralyzing pressure of trying to pick the "perfect" path. Instead, he reveals that fulfillment comes from having faith in your choices and putting everything into making them the right decision, ultimately transforming setbacks into powerful opportunities for purpose, leadership, and serving others.
